title: Oshaya Zeira, one of the academy’s members
author: Aharon Hyman
attribution: Model-assisted translation, editorially reviewed; publication authorized by Joshua Waxman.

paragraphs: In Taanit 24a: It is told that in the house of the Nasi they decreed a fast, and rain did not come. Oshaya Zeira, one of the academy’s members, taught them: "A bride whose eyes are beautiful does not need her whole body examined." The servants of the Resh Galuta came and troubled him. The townspeople said to them: He insults and troubles us too, but we saw that everything he does he does for the sake of Heaven, and therefore we leave him alone; so you too, leave him alone. (And Rashi explains: because he was the youngest in the yeshiva, and they called him this because there was another Oshaya.) And in Chullin 31a: Rava said: "What Oshaya Zeira, one of the academy’s members, taught" — he taught it and he also said it: the halakha follows Rabbi Natan. (And Rashi explains: the youngest of the yeshiva; Rashi continues: “It seems to me that he was called Oshaya Zeira”, and 'demin chavraya' means that he was among the members of the academy; and in Tosafot, 'Avimi, one of the academy’s members'.) And in Niddah 26a we find: "It was taught: Rabbi Oshaya Zeira, one of the academy’s members"; Hyman says it must be emended to "Oshaya taught." Hyman considers it very likely that he is the second Rav Oshaya, and because he was only a haver and not ordained, they called him thus; and it was Rav Oshaya's way to cite baraitot, as mentioned in his entry.

notes.text: Rashi on Chullin31a himself gives both the youngest-in-the-academy explanation and the alternative “Oshaya Zeira, one of the academy’s members.” The first-person alternative belongs to Rashi’s cited comment; Hyman’s subsequent Rav Oshaya identification and proposed reciter formula remain his own.

The two explanations, including the alternative beginning “It seems to me,” belong to the consulted Rashi Chullin 31a. Hyman’s proposed reciter formula, lack-of-ordination explanation and identification with the second Rav Oshaya remain attributed to him; a reciter’s function does not itself establish a Mishnaic date.
